passage: Manjula took the early bus to the tehsil office for an income certificate and joined a queue that turned out to be the wrong one. A man at counter two sent her to counter five. Counter five said the form was at counter two. A peon said, "Come tomorrow." She went home with nothing and a headache. That evening her friend Payal, who worked at a village service centre, said, "Ask what to bring before you go, and carry the originals plus two sets of photocopies." Manjula phoned the office and wrote the list in her notebook: ration card, school leaving certificate, address proof, photographs. She left at six the next morning, stood first in the queue, and by noon the clerk had stamped her form and said, "Come Friday for the certificate."

qa.q: Which counter did the man at counter two send Manjula to?
qa.a: He sent her to counter five.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel after being sent between counters and told to come tomorrow?
qa.a: Lost and frustrated, since she went home with nothing and a headache.

qa.q: What preparation made the second trip work?
qa.a: Phoning ahead for the list, carrying originals plus two sets of photocopies, and leaving at six to stand first in the queue.

qa.q: How might Payal's job at the village service centre have shaped the advice given?
qa.a: Payal knows how offices work from the job, so gave practical advice: ask what to bring and carry originals and photocopies.

grounding: Shows a young adult lost among counters and conflicting advice at a certificate office, then succeeding by asking in advance and bringing originals and copies.

passage: Astrid, twenty and new in the city, went to the town hall to update the address on her ID card. Numbers flashed on screens, there were three counters, and the signs were in a language she half knew. A woman sent her to counter B. Counter B said address forms were upstairs. Upstairs asked for proof of tenancy, which she had left at home. She stood in the corridor feeling lost. Back at the flat, her flatmate Lars said he had done the same task last spring and wrote her a list: passport, tenancy contract, one photocopy of each, opening hours checked on the website. The next Tuesday she arrived at eight, before the queue, with two folders. It took fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What did Lars write on the list for Astrid?
qa.a: Lars listed passport, tenancy contract, one photocopy of each, and opening hours checked on the website.

qa.q: What was Astrid feeling in the corridor after being sent from counter to counter?
qa.a: Lost and unsure, since the signs were in a language she only half knew and she lacked proof of tenancy.

qa.q: What could Astrid do on a second visit so she would not be sent away again?
qa.a: Arrive early with the originals and copies in folders, as she did, after checking opening hours.

qa.q: How might Lars have seen Astrid's trouble at the town hall?
qa.a: Lars remembered doing the same task last spring, so probably understood the confusion and offered a helpful list.

grounding: Shows a young adult confused by queues and counters at an office, then saving trips by preparing originals, copies and hours.

passage:
My name is Pallavi, and last year I went to the municipal office three times for one birth certificate correction.
The first time, I reached at noon. The guard pointed me to counter four. Counter four sent me to counter seven. Counter seven said, "Bring a photocopy of your mother's ID," and shut the window for lunch. I stood in the corridor feeling stupid and close to tears.
The second time I had the photocopy, but not the original. A different clerk wanted both.
Before the third trip, I called my neighbour Seema aunty, who had done the same correction for her son. She dictated a list: originals, two photocopies of each, passport photos, the affidavit. She told me to reach before the doors opened. I did. I was fourth in line, and I was out by eleven.
Now I ask for a list before I go anywhere.

qa.q: Which counter did the guard point Pallavi to first?
qa.a: The guard pointed Pallavi to counter four.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel standing in the corridor on the first trip?
qa.a: Pallavi felt lost and humiliated, close to tears after being passed between counters.

qa.q: What made the third trip work?
qa.a: Getting a full document list from someone who had done it, bringing originals and photocopies, and reaching before the doors opened.

qa.q: What is it like for Seema aunty to get Pallavi's call?
qa.a: Seema aunty seems glad to help, sharing a clear list from her own experience with her son's correction.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult confused by counters and conflicting advice at an office who saves trips by asking in advance and going early with documents.

passage:
Help-desk note, regional transport office, Thursday.
A young man, Sachin, came to the desk at 2:40 holding a single photocopy. He had come to change the address on his licence. He told me he had already been to counters two, five and nine. Counter nine had said the online appointment slip was needed; counter two had said it wasn't. His shirt was damp and he kept apologising.
I asked him to sit. I wrote down, in order, what he needed: the appointment slip, original licence, original address proof, one photocopy of each. He had the licence. The address proof was at home.
He looked ready to give up. I told him the office opens at 9:30 and the queue is shortest before ten. He took a photo of my list. My colleague Nikita printed him a slip for Monday. I will look out for him then.
— Help-desk volunteer, Dhanush

qa.q: Which counters had Sachin already been to?
qa.a: He had already been to counters two, five and nine.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling at the desk, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sachin was flustered and discouraged; his shirt was damp, he kept apologising and he looked ready to give up.

qa.q: What did the help desk do that saved Sachin more wasted trips?
qa.a: They wrote a clear list of every document in order, told him the best time to come, and printed an appointment slip for Monday.

qa.q: If you were Sachin, what would you want from counter nine?
qa.a: A clear list of what to bring on the first visit, instead of advice that clashed with counter two.

grounding: Shows a young adult lost among counters and conflicting advice at a transport office, helped by a clear document list and advice to come early.

passage:
Wednesday night.
Taluk office, round two. Round one was last Friday, when I waited three hours and then learned the domicile form needed a stamped ration card copy I did not have.
Today was better, but only because of Swati. She got hers done in June. Yesterday she sent me a photo of her folder: originals in one pocket, two photocopies of everything in the other, a spare passport photo taped inside. "Reach by nine, Joseph. The line doubles after ten."
I reached at 8:50. Counter one gave me a token. Counter three checked my papers and said the photocopy was too faint. I nearly lost it. Then I remembered Swati's folder, pulled out the second copy, and the clerk nodded.
Receipt in hand by 11:15. Collect on the 20th. I am writing Swati's list inside my notebook cover so I never do round one again.

qa.q: What time did the narrator reach the taluk office today?
qa.a: The narrator reached at 8:50.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when the clerk said the photocopy was too faint?
qa.a: Joseph felt frustrated and close to losing his temper, until Joseph remembered the spare copy and relief took over.

qa.q: What small step from this entry would help anyone going to a government office?
qa.a: Carrying originals plus two photocopies of everything and reaching before the queue grows, as Swati advised.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when she hears it went smoothly?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that her folder photo saved Joseph another wasted trip.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who wastes one trip to a government office, then goes early with originals and photocopies after asking what to bring.
